client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately because I failed two exams this semester, and now I'm anxious about whether I'll even graduate on time. Every time I think about it, my heart races, and I can't shake the feeling that I'm letting everyone down. I honestly wonder if therapy can really help me with this kind of pressure.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a heavy load right now with those feelings of overwhelm and anxiety about your exams and graduation. I hear how much pressure you’re feeling, and it’s understandable to wonder if therapy can really support you through this. Can you share more about what you think therapy might help you with, or what you hope to gain from it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think therapy could help me manage my anxiety a bit better, maybe give me some tools to cope with all this pressure. But part of me wonders if it’s really going to make a difference. I mean, what if I still feel just as overwhelmed after trying some techniques? It feels like the stress is just too much to handle right now.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling a mix of hope and skepticism about therapy, which is completely valid. It’s understandable to doubt whether techniques can truly help when the stress feels so overwhelming. What specific concerns do you have about trying these coping tools, and what would it look like for you if they did help even a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess my biggest concern is that I might try the coping tools, and they just won’t work for me. I can already hear that inner voice telling me I’m not doing it right or that it’s pointless. If they did help even a little, maybe I would feel more in control of my anxiety, but I just can't see how that would happen with everything weighing on my mind.
therapist: It seems like your inner voice is really critical, creating a lot of doubt about trying new coping tools. It’s completely normal to feel that way, especially when everything feels so heavy. Can we explore together what those thoughts say about your expectations for yourself and how you might be able to challenge them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess my expectations are really high because I feel like I should just be able to handle all this pressure without falling apart. When I think about challenging those thoughts, it feels daunting—like I’m just going to end up disappointing myself again. It’s hard to believe I can change that inner voice when it feels like it’s been there forever, constantly reminding me of my failures.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling a lot of pressure to meet high expectations, and that inner voice is really weighing on you. It’s understandable to feel daunted when it seems like that voice has been around for so long, reminding you of past failures. What if we took a step back and considered what small, manageable changes might look like, rather than trying to tackle everything at once?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I see what you're saying about taking small steps, but I still worry that even those won’t be enough to make a difference. It feels like every little change would just end up being another thing I have to stress about. Honestly, I struggle to even think of what those small changes could be, and it feels overwhelming to try to figure it out on my own.
therapist: It sounds like you’re feeling really stuck right now, and the idea of even small changes feels like just another source of stress. That’s completely understandable, especially when everything feels so overwhelming. What if we brainstormed some tiny, manageable steps together? It might help to have someone to share the load with as you explore this.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate the idea of brainstorming together, but I still feel kind of lost about what those small steps could even be. It’s hard to see how anything I do would make a real difference when I’m facing such big challenges, like those exams. I guess I just worry that even with support, I’ll still end up feeling overwhelmed and stuck in the same place.
therapist: I hear you feeling lost and overwhelmed, especially when it comes to figuring out small steps forward. It’s tough to see how anything you do could make a real difference when you're facing such significant challenges. Can we take a moment to think about what little things have helped you in the past, even if they feel small? Sometimes reflecting on past successes, no matter how minor, can spark ideas for the present.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think about it, and there have been a few times when I managed to study a bit more effectively, like creating a schedule or breaking things into smaller chunks. But even those feel like they were just lucky breaks rather than something I can rely on. I worry that if I try to do that again, I might fail and just end up feeling worse. It's tough to believe that reflecting on those moments will actually help me now.
therapist: It’s great that you’re recognizing moments when you’ve studied more effectively, even if they feel like lucky breaks. It’s completely natural to worry about trying again and facing disappointment, especially when the stakes feel high. What if we looked at those past experiences not just as luck, but as evidence that you have the ability to create a structure that works for you? How might it feel to approach those strategies as something you can build on, rather than a test of success or failure?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I can see your point about viewing those moments as evidence of my ability to create a structure, but it still feels hard to shake off that fear of failure. I can’t help but think that if I try to build on those strategies and it doesn’t work this time, I’ll just feel even worse about myself. It’s like I’m stuck in this cycle of wanting to try but being scared of what happens if I don’t succeed.
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught in a really difficult place, wanting to try but feeling afraid of what might happen if things don’t go as planned. That fear of failure can be really paralyzing, especially when you’ve put so much pressure on yourself. What do you think it would look like to give yourself permission to try without the weight of needing to succeed? How might that shift your perspective on the process?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess giving myself permission to try without the pressure of needing to succeed sounds freeing, but it also feels really foreign to me. I always tie my worth and my success to the outcomes, so letting go of that feels like I’d be losing part of myself. I'm not sure how to even start thinking that way, especially when I've always been so focused on results.
therapist: It’s understandable that letting go of the focus on outcomes feels foreign and even a bit scary. Tying your worth to results is something many people struggle with, and it can be tough to imagine redefining that. What if we explored what success could look like if it wasn’t solely based on outcomes? How might you feel about celebrating the effort you put in, regardless of the result?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Celebrating the effort instead of just the results is a nice idea, but it feels really challenging for me to wrap my head around. I’ve always been taught that success is about what you achieve, so it’s hard to break that mindset. I guess I worry that if I focus too much on the effort, it might just lead to complacency, and then I won't push myself enough when I really need to.
therapist: It’s completely understandable that shifting your mindset to celebrate effort instead of just results feels challenging, especially when you’ve been taught to equate success with achievement. Your concern about complacency is valid, and it’s important to find a balance that allows you to push yourself while also recognizing the value in your efforts. What if we explored small ways to acknowledge your efforts without losing sight of your goals? How might that look for you in your studying or daily routines?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
